judgments.title: PENGERANG REFINING COMPANY SDN. BHD. v MAJLIS PERBANDARAN PENGERANG
judgments.catchwords: Administrative Law – Judicial review – Duty of candour – Public authority – Duty to make full and fair disclosure of all material facts – Failure to disclose that Valuation List being amended had expired – Breach of duty of candour – Consequences. Local Government Law – Valuation List – Statutory lifespan – Section 137 Local Government Act 1976 – New Valuation List must be prepared once every five years – Valuation List expires after five years – No local authority may use Valuation List for indeterminable period. Local Government Law – Valuation List – Amendment – Section 144 Local Government Act 1976 – Amendment can only be made to current Valuation List – Not to expired or outdated Valuation List – Amendment to expired list is ultra vires and void. Local Government Law – Valuation List – Section 137(2) – Saving provision – Valuation List remains in force until superseded by new list – Not a power to extend lifespan of existing list – Only temporary measure while new list being prepared– Extension of time – Section 137(3) – State Authority may extend period for preparation of new Valuation List – Not power to extend validity of existing Valuation List – No extension granted in present case. Local Government Law – Retrospective rates – Amendment to current Valuation List may have retrospective effect – But no retrospective effect where Valuation List itself has expired – Question of retrospectivity becomes academic.

judgments.title: OCEAN GLORY SEAFOOD SDN. BHD. v GCH RETAIL (MALAYSIA) SDN BHD
judgments.catchwords: Breach of Contract – Claim arising from a failure to perform obligations under alleged agreements – Condition Precedent – Performance obligations for specific tranches of goods being conditional upon the issuance of individual Purchase Orders (POs) – Whether binding contracts were formed via email correspondence, and if the subsequent obligation to perform was subject to a condition precedent requiring individual Purchase Orders – Course of Dealing – A long-standing history of transactions qualifying the mode and mechanics of contract performance - Liability for Outstanding Invoices – Whether the Defendant is legally liable to pay the sum of RM 891,879.60 for a delivered shipment (FCL-2) where a Purchase Order was issued and receipt was independently proven. Adverse Inference – Invocation of Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act 1950 for a party's failure to call a material witness within their knowledge and control. Strict Adherence to Pleadings – Restricting parties to their pleaded case and preventing courts from awarding remedies on unpleaded material facts or claims – Unpleaded Set-Off – An unpleaded substantive defence raised during oral testimony to reduce or extinguish a debt claim, which is legally untenable – Recovery of Unpleaded and Unproven Losses – Whether the Plaintiff is entitled to recover damages for the alleged destruction of expired inventory when the destruction was neither pleaded nor supported by documentary evidence – Viability of an Unpleaded Set-Off Defence – Whether the Defendant can legally rely on an unpleaded overpayment from a separate suit as a valid set-off defence to defeat a debt claim. Computer-Generated Documents – The admissibility of system-printed documents under Section 90A of the Evidence Act 1950 – Hearsay Evidence – Documents tendered to prove the truth of their contents without calling the actual maker to testify – Admissibility of Digital Records Without Statutory Certificates – Whether computer-generated Goods Receiving Notes (GRNs) are admissible as primary evidence in the absence of a compliance certificate under Section 90A of the Evidence Act 1950 – Evidential Weight of Hearsay Documents – What evidential weight should be accorded to a commercial quotation when the named maker is not called to testify at trial. Mitigation of Loss – The duty of an aggrieved party to mitigate damages, including the equitable requirement to give notice to the defaulting party before conducting a mitigation sale – Whether the Plaintiff can claim mitigation losses from an on-sale to a third party when it failed to provide prior notice to the Defendant and failed to produce documentary proof of the sale.

CRIMINAL LAW (DANGEROUS DRUGS) CRIMINAL LAW: Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 – Section 39A(2)(d) – Possession – Consolidated charge combining weights of heroin and monoacetylmorphines – Single transaction – Whether separate drug types recovered from the same physical transaction must be charged under distinct counts – Binding precedential force of the Court of Appeal in Abd Talib bin Bakri lwn Pendakwa Raya [2020] 3 MLJ 777 – Purpose of aggregation – Prevention of consecutive, compounding statutory double-presumptions under the Act – Protection of equality before the law under Article 8(1) of the Federal Constitution. 2. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE (REVISION & INHERENT POWERS) CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Revision – Powers of High Court – Supervisory and revisionary jurisdiction – Criminal Procedure Code, s. 323 – Courts of Judicature Act 1964, ss. 31, 35(1) – Sessions Court Judge summarily discharging accused under a Discharge Not Amounting to Acquittal (DNAA) on a mention date – Preliminary objection regarding the structure of the charge sheet – Whether subordinate courts possess inherent power to abort trials or strike out valid charges – Distinction between inherent jurisdiction of superior courts and limited statutory jurisdiction of subordinate judiciaries – Application of Karpal Singh & Anor v. Public Prosecutor [1991] 2 MLJ 544. 3. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE (JOINT TRIAL & TRANSFER) CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Trial – Joint trial – Criminal Procedure Code, s. 170 – Same transaction doctrine – Application by the prosecution to try a reinstated Section 39A(2) Sessions Court charge jointly with a Section 12(2) Magistrate's Court minor charge – Offences arising from the same narcotics raid – Unity of time, place, community of purpose and continuity of action – Duplication of witnesses and chemist testimonies – Whether separate trials create a risk of inconsistent findings of fact – Proper administration of justice – Criminal Procedure Code, s. 417. 4. CONSTITUTIONAL LAW (SEPARATION OF POWERS) CONSTITUTIONAL LAW: Public Prosecutor – Executive discretion – Federal Constitution, art. 145(3) – Absolute control and direction of criminal prosecutions – Framing and preference of charges – Whether subordinate courts can interfere with the prosecutorial choice of charges – Separation of powers – Courts as gatekeepers of statutory legality vs. directors of prosecution – Application of Long bin Samad & Ors. v. Public Prosecutor [1974] 2 MLJ 152. 5. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION (RULES OF CONSTRUCTION) STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rules of construction – Literal rule – Purposive approach – Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s. 17A – Phrase "a total of 5 grammes or more in weight of heroin, morphine and monoacetylmorphines" – Conjunctive word "and" – Explicit statutory authorisation to aggregate weights of specified substances – Whether court has power to fill statutory gaps or rewrite clear penal provisions under the guise of equity – Application of Gan Joon Zin v. Fong Kui Lun & Ors [2004] 4 CLJ 729. 6. WORDS & PHRASES WORDS & PHRASES: "total of 5 grammes or more in weight of heroin, morphine and monoacetylmorphines" – Section 39A(2)(d) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 – Literal and grammatical construction. judgments.title: Cheong Hwee Ling v Leong Pit Tee & ors
judgments.catchwords: Pre- nuptial agreement – whether agreement is valid and binding as the matter of law – Section 56 of the Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 – Court is of the view that legislative intention underlying Section 56 of the Act cannot be given full effect until the requisite rules are promulgated- until rules are enacted pursuant to Section 56 of the Act, pre-nuptial and post-nuptial agreements cannot be regarded as valid, admissible and enforceable for the purposes of matrimonial proceedings under the Act – the word “may” in Section 56 of the Act does not confer an unfettered discretion upon the court or litigants to disregard the procedural framework contemplated by the legislator – In the present case, the Agreement relied upon by the parties cannot presently be accorded validity or enforceability under the Act.
